title: Rereading is the worst way to study

lines.text: Rereading your notes is one of the *worst* ways to study. | Here are *four* things the research found instead.
First, a study from *2006.* | Students either *reread* a passage, or *tested* themselves on it.
One week later, | the testers remembered *sixty-one* percent. | The rereaders? *Forty.*
Second, the rereaders felt *more* confident. | Rereading feels like learning, | because the words look *familiar.* | Your brain mistakes *I've seen this* | for *I know this.*
Third, a review of *118* studies | found practice tests beat the *other* ways of studying, | again and again.
And finally, *feedback.* | When people checked the right answer straight after testing themselves, | the benefit nearly *doubled.*
So close the notes, | *quiz* yourself, | and check your answers *right away.*
If you want lessons that make you do exactly that, | a few minutes a day, | the app is in my *bio.* | It's called *Teyro.*

sources: Roediger & Karpicke (2006), Psychological Science: one-week recall 61% (repeated testing) vs 40% (repeated study); repeated-study group predicted better recall
Adesope, Trevisan & Sundararajan (2017), Review of Educational Research: 272 effect sizes from 118 articles, practice tests g = 0.61
Rowland (2014), Psychological Bulletin: testing effect g = 0.73 with feedback vs 0.39 without
